units.name: request-model
units.role: Define what an HTTP request and response are as objects, and dispatch hooks on them.
units.description: This is the part of the library that understands what a web request and a web response actually are. You give it a web address, a method, and some options (headers, form data, files, cookies), and it builds a fully-formed request ready to be sent, encoding everything the way an HTTP server expects. When a reply comes back, it wraps the raw bytes in a Response object so a caller can ask simple questions like 'did it succeed?', 'what did it say?', or 'what cookies did the server set?'. It also runs any callback functions ('hooks') the caller registered to run when a response is produced. It never opens a network connection itself — it hands that job to the transport layer and only shapes the data going in and coming out.

units.description: This is the very first thing a person touches when they use the library: simple functions like get(url), post(url, data=...), and friends. Each one just opens a temporary session, makes the one request, and returns the response. This unit also includes the package's own startup code, which checks that the installed versions of a few key dependencies (the network engine and encoding-detection libraries) are compatible with each other, warns the user if they are not, patches in an alternate secure-connection implementation on Python installations that need it, and gathers together every name (functions, classes, exceptions, the status-code table) that makes up the library's public interface.

units.name: session-orchestration
units.role: Conduct the end-to-end lifecycle of a request: merge settings, prepare it, send it, follow redirects, save cookies.
units.description: This is the conductor that makes a simple call like session.get(url) do the right thing end to end. It takes whatever the caller asked for on this one call and combines it with the defaults saved on the session (headers, cookies, authentication, proxies, trust settings), builds the outgoing request, hands it to the transport layer to actually be sent, and then decides what to do with the reply: follow any redirect the server asked for (carefully deciding whether to keep sending the same credentials and body along the way), save any cookies the server set, and run any callbacks the caller registered. It is the layer that turns individual pieces — a request shape, a cookie jar, an auth scheme, a network transport — into one coherent conversation with a server, optionally reused across many calls.

units.name: http-transport
units.role: Actually open connections and move bytes to and from a server.
units.description: This is the part of the library that talks to the real network. It takes a fully-prepared request and, using the third-party urllib3 engine, opens a plain or proxied (and optionally SOCKS or TLS) connection, sends the request, waits for the reply, and translates urllib3's raw answer back into the Response object the rest of the library understands. It decides which certificate bundle to trust for verifying secure sites, and turns low-level network failures (timeouts, broken connections, bad certificates) into the library's own well-known error types.

units.name: cookie-jar
units.role: Wrap the stdlib cookie jar so cookies can be read/written like a dict, and convert between jars, dicts, and headers.
units.description: This unit manages HTTP cookies. Python already has a built-in way to store cookies correctly (respecting domain, path, and expiry rules), but it isn't convenient to use directly, so this unit wraps it in something that behaves like an ordinary dictionary — you can do jar['session_id'] just like a dict, while the correctness rules are still enforced underneath. It also provides small helper functions to build a single cookie from raw pieces, copy or merge cookie jars together, pull the cookies out of a server's reply into a jar, and turn a jar's contents into the 'Cookie' header line to send on the next request.

units.name: auth
units.role: Encode the schemes by which a request proves who is making it (Basic, Digest, Proxy).
units.description: This unit teaches the library how a request can prove its identity before it's sent. It covers HTTP Basic authentication (a username and password encoded into a header), Proxy authentication (the same idea, aimed at a proxy server in front of the real destination), and HTTP Digest authentication (a more elaborate back-and-forth where the server issues a challenge and the client computes a cryptographic answer using the credentials and some randomness). Each scheme is a small object that, handed a not-yet-sent request, stamps the right authentication header onto it — Digest auth goes further and automatically resends the request once it sees a '401 Unauthorized' challenge from the server.

None of these functions hold state of their own; every other part of the library that builds, sends, or manages requests calls into this toolbox.

units.name: compat-layer
units.role: Isolate the rest of the library from Python/urllib3/optional-dependency differences, and hold shared typing definitions.
units.description: This is the library's internal glue layer. It hides differences between versions of Python, the underlying network engine (urllib3), and optional dependencies (which text-encoding-detector or JSON library happens to be installed) so the rest of the code can be written once. It exposes standard-library URL and cookie helpers under stable names, re-publishes the third-party network and internationalized-domain-name libraries as requests.packages.* for old code that expects them there, and defines a private catalogue of type descriptions that programming tools use to catch mistakes before the code runs, but which have no effect while the program is actually executing.

units.name: data-structures
units.role: Two small, generic, reusable containers with no HTTP-specific behavior and no effects.
units.description: This unit provides two small general-purpose containers used throughout the library. The first is a dictionary that treats keys like 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' as the same key, which matches how HTTP headers are defined to behave, and is used everywhere headers are stored or compared. The second is a dictionary that returns nothing instead of raising an error when you ask for a key it doesn't have; it's used to build the single lookup table that lets code refer to HTTP status codes by friendly names (like 'not_found') instead of bare numbers (like 404). Neither structure touches the network, the filesystem, or any other part of the outside world.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: Catalog every error and warning condition the library can signal to a caller.
units.description: This part of the library defines the complete vocabulary of things that can go wrong when it tries to make an HTTP call on your behalf: a connection failure, a timeout, too many redirects, a malformed URL, an SSL problem, a response that isn't valid JSON, and so on. Rather than doing any work itself, it is a catalog of named error and warning types arranged in a family tree (a timeout, for example, is also a kind of connection error), so other parts of the library can raise a precise, meaningful error, and so a caller can catch exactly the failure they care about, or catch one broad type to cover everything the library might raise.

violations_observed.note: `from . import utils` re-exports the entire utils module as `requests.utils` for external callers, rather than depending on one named entrypoint. Similarly `from . import packages` re-exports the whole compat-layer packages shim as `requests.packages`. This is a deliberate whole-module re-export pattern, not a mistake, but it means the dependency can't be pinned to a single entrypoint the way the contract model expects.

_types.py imports PreparedRequest, Response, RequestsCookieJar, AuthBase, and CaseInsensitiveDict from domain/infra units purely for TYPE_CHECKING-only type aliases. This makes compat-layer (which every other unit depends on for typing) textually reference those units back, but the reference is erased at runtime and creates no real import cycle — flagged here because it inverts the usual 'foundational layer has no dependents' expectation.
